title: European chemicals won the quarter, not the war
gist: Oxford Economics argues that European chemical producers' post-Middle East-conflict earnings bounce reflects Asian rivals' feedstock disruption rather than improved European competitiveness, with 12-month EBITDA still roughly a quarter below 2019. Rising European gas prices and record-low EU gas storage for the season should erode Europe's cost advantage, and the firm now expects European chemicals output to contract in 2027 versus a pre-conflict forecast of 1.4% growth.

themes.theme: Europe's chemicals rebound is borrowed from rivals' disruption

insights.claim: Since the Middle East conflict began, European chemical producers' earnings have picked up, but 12-month EBITDA at key manufacturers remains roughly a quarter below its 2019 level.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: The rally in European chemicals earnings starts from a deeply depressed base, limiting re-rating upside.
insights.quote: 12-month EBITDA at key manufactures remains roughly a quarter below its 2019 level
insights.locator: Since the conflict in the Middle East began

insights.claim: Oxford Economics contends that the European chemicals earnings gains reflect competitors' problems rather than any meaningful improvement in Europe's own competitive position, and are unlikely to last.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Pushes back on the consensus 'Europe as conflict beneficiary' trade; suggests fading the rebound in European chemicals.
insights.quote: We think the gains reflect their competitors’ problems rather than any meaningful improvement in Europe’s own position, and that they are unlikely to last.
insights.locator: Since the conflict in the Middle East began

insights.claim: Asian chemical producers are short on feedstock and face steeper cost increases because their sectors rely heavily on oil and naphtha imported from the Middle East, prompting some buyers to switch to European suppliers that could still deliver.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Identifies Asian naphtha-based crackers as the most exposed to Middle East supply disruption, and the source of Europe's temporary market-share gain.
insights.quote: their chemicals sectors rely heavily on oil and naphtha imported from the Middle East, some buyers have turned to European suppliers who could still deliver

themes.theme: Energy cost gap with Asia narrowing

insights.claim: Oxford Economics' implied energy cost index shows the chemicals cost gap between Europe and Asia narrowing.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: A relative energy-cost metric is the key gauge for whether Europe's competitive window stays open.
insights.quote: Our implied energy cost index shows the gap with Asia narrowing.

insights.claim: European gas prices are rising ahead of winter and EU gas storage is at its lowest level for this time of year in more than a decade.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Tight EU gas storage into winter implies upside risk to European gas prices and energy-intensive producers' costs.
insights.quote: EU gas storage at its lowest level for this time of year in more than a decade

insights.claim: European chemicals costs are set to fall less steeply than Asian costs in 2027, eroding Europe's early competitive advantage from the conflict.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: Relative cost normalization in 2027 favors Asian producers recovering share from European chemicals.
insights.quote: European costs are set to fall less steeply than Asia in 2027, eroding Europe’s early advantage

insights.claim: Oxford Economics now expects European chemicals output to contract in 2027, having forecast growth of 1.4% for that year before the Middle East conflict.
insights.speaker: Sally Li
insights.so_what: A swing from +1.4% growth to contraction signals downside to 2027 volume and earnings estimates for European chemicals.
insights.quote: We now expect European chemicals output to contract in 2027, having forecast growth of 1.4% for the year before the conflict.
